Trezor Investigation Update: Malicious Circuit Boards Found in Three Safe 5 Wallets

Hardware wallet manufacturer Trezor provided an update on its investigation into hardware tampering involving devices sold by reseller CryptoBilis. After inspecting devices from 48 users who contacted the company, Trezor confirmed that three Trezor Safe 5 wallets sold between August 20 and September 23, 2026, through CryptoBilis and its Tokopedia and Shopee stores contained malicious circuit boards. The implants, concealed between the motherboard and display, could capture recovery seeds and passphrases shown on the screen and transmit them to attackers’ servers via cellular networks. No user funds have been reported stolen to date. Trezor has reduced its reseller network by approximately 80%, tightened procurement and warehousing controls, and released firmware version 2.13.1 on November 11 to block data capture by the identified implants. Customers who purchased devices from CryptoBilis since March 2026 are eligible for a free replacement or refund. — link

--- From rss ---
Crypto wallet firm Trezor has cut its reseller network by 80% following the discovery of more spy implants in devices sold by Malaysian vendor CryptoBilis.
Trezor’s latest update on the spyware incident revealed it has implemented stricter rules for vendors in order to protect its supply chain.
However, only 20% of vendors were able to abide by the new rules that focus on “how devices are sourced, stored and who has access to them.”
Trezor stressed, however, that the dropped resellers “were trustworthy and posed no immediate threat.”
Trezor says its new update renders spy implants useless
Trezor also claims to have released an update on November 11 that stops the implants recording data and renders them “useless.”
A spokesperson for the company told Protos, “The implant listens to the communication between the MCU and the display and triggers the capture when it sees a specific sequence.”
In order to stop the sequence trigger, which is a wallet’s seed phrase, Trezor claims it “changed the order of the commands sent to the display” and that it can do this “without any effect on the displayed screen.”
Read more: Trezor reveals Malaysian reseller sold wallet with spyware
Despite this, Trezor warned CryptoBilis customers that they should still move their funds to a new wallet as “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.”
Three Trezor wallets infected but no funds stolen
Trezor says a total of three Trezor Safe 5 models have been found implanted with the spyware and that the devices were purchased between August 20 and September 23.
It still maintains that no crypto has been stolen from the affected devices, and has offered those who bought their wallets from CryptoBilis a free replacement.
Ledger wallet users suffered $86M theft
Wallets sold by Trezor rival Ledger were drained of over $86 million last month in an attack that also involved tampered wallets sold by CryptoBilis.
Stablecoin firm Tether froze $10 million in stolen funds, and Ledger asked multiple wallet vendors across Asia to halt sales.
Read more: Ledger roasted over $849 device launch after $86M hack
Its investigation uncovered an organized crime group spending millions to build spyware infrastructure that involved logistics, seed collector servers, and draining/laundering infrastructure.
It took several weeks before Trezor revealed it too had discovered an implant in one of its devices.

The second-half integration would add another network to a service already live on Canton and DTCC's private Besu blockchain.

--- From rss ---
In brief
- The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana, with tokenized assets expected on the network in the second half of 2027.
- The service, which launched on October 28, creates tokenized versions of DTC-held securities including Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and U.S. Treasuries.
- DTCC said tokens on Solana will carry the same investor protections and ownership rights as traditionally held securities.
The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the backbone of U.S. securities settlement, plans to bring its tokenized securities to Solana, it announced on Thursday.
The firm will connect the DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) to the Solana network, allowing eligible assets held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be converted into tokens on Solana. The integration is planned for the second half of 2027.
BREAKING: @The_DTCC to tokenize custodied assets on Solana. announced plans to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service to Solana, enabling the tokenization of eligible DTC-custodied assets on the network.
The integration is planned for the second half of 2027, further advancing… pic.twitter.com/gXszWFgUOX
— Solana (@solana) November 12, 2026
"DTCC is bringing regulated, DTC-tokenized securities to another major blockchain ecosystem, giving market participants greater choice in where they access and utilize tokenized assets," DTCC CEO Frank La Salla said.
DTS went live on October 28 on the Canton Network and DTCC's own private blockchain, built on the Besu framework, with more networks due to be added in 2027, according to DTCC's launch announcement. The service creates tokenized "digital twins" of securities held at DTC, which custodies more than $114 trillion in assets. Solana joins Stellar and Circle's Arc blockchain, which are expected to be added in 2027, according to a DTCC fact sheet.
Under a no-action letter from the SEC, the service is limited to a defined set of highly liquid assets, including Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasuries. Morgan Stanley said last week it had tokenized U.S. stocks and Treasuries through the service.
Tokens issued on Solana "will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.
Will HYPE flip SOL in 2026?
Solana's institutional push
Solana has been actively courting traditional finance in recent months, with Solana Foundation head of institutional Nick Ducoff arguing that, "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale." He added that institutions are "already issuing, settling and deploying capital" on the network, in a tweet shared by Solana's official account.
Last month, the Solana Foundation unveiled an open standard for institutional settlement developed with input from J.P. Morgan, and the network completed its Alpenglow upgrade, cutting the time it takes for transactions to become final to roughly 150 milliseconds.
Solana is also lining up more venues for tokenized stocks. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on Solana, starting with Galaxy and Forward Industries.

DTCC Plans Solana Expansion as Wallet Rules Limit Access
The US securities clearinghouse plans to bring tokenized stocks to Solana in 2027, but analysts say restrictions could limit adoption.
Plans by the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation’s (DTCC) to bring tokenized securities to Solana could attract more traditional financial institutions to the blockchain, but regulatory restrictions may limit the impact on the network, according to analysts.
DTCC announced Thursday that it plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027. The move would allow certain securities held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be turned into digital tokens on the network.
Solana is a blockchain known for its fast transactions and low fees, making it popular for crypto trading, especially memecoins. The network had about $4.94 billion in total value locked (TVL) as of Nov. 12, according to DefiLlama.
Experts say the move could help Solana attract more activity beyond just memecoins, but it’s not clear how much new capital and transaction volume it could bring to the network. What’s more, current US regulatory rules still limit who can hold and transfer the tokenized assets.
Memes paved the way
Alex Lin, founding partner at venture capital firm Reforge, said Solana’s history of handling large amounts of memecoin trading may have helped show that the network can support traditional financial activity.
“Memes were a public stress test that gave Solana credibility that it can handle retail-scale volume cheaply and reliably,” Lin told Cointelegraph. “The casino paved the way for more institutional plumbing.”
However, under a December 2025 SEC no-action letter, DTC participants must register wallets to hold tokenized securities. The tokens can only be transferred between registered wallets, potentially limiting usage.
“It’s overstated in the near term because the SEC relief from Dec 2025 keeps these tokens in a walled garden of registered DTC participants, so permissionless retail and DeFi liquidity can’t touch these tokens directly yet,” Lin said. “Regulators need to let these assets work as true onchain collateral and that’s more policy than tech.”
DTCC launched its tokenization service on the Canton Network and its private Besu network on Oct. 28, allowing certain securities to be turned into digital tokens while keeping the same investor protections. At launch, DTCC said 20 DTC participants had signed agreements to access the service, but it has not said whether any plan to use Solana.
Cointelegraph contacted DTCC and the Solana Foundation for additional comments but has not yet heard back.
Related: Robinhood’s Tenev warns US tokenization uncertainty deters ‘serious assets’
Solana trading slows, but tokenized assets grow
Kha Nguyen, CEO and co-founder of blockchain analytics platform Birdeye, which tracks trading activity on Solana, said the blockchain has already seen growing demand for tokenized stocks without DTCC’s involvement.
According to Birdeye’s H1 2026 report, tokenized-stock trading volume on Solana reached around $4.9 billion in the first half of the year, more than six times the volume recorded in the previous six months.
Birdeye’s third-quarter report also found that more than 1 million accounts held tokenized stocks on Solana by late September.
Still, broader trading activity on Solana has slowed with the network recording about 6.9 billion transactions in the 30 days ending Nov. 11, down almost 40% from the previous 30-day period, according to Token Terminal data. Meanwhile, trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) fell 34.4% to $39.1 billion, while monthly active addresses dropped nearly 13% to 45.8 million.
Network fees also fell 39% to about $17 million over the same period. However, the value of tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) on Solana rose almost 7% to $4.76 billion as of Nov. 11 – up from $4.46 billion on Oct. 12.
“By late September more than a million wallets had held a tokenized stock, and real-world assets on Solana had grown five times in a year,” Nguyen told Cointelegraph.
Nguyen said bringing more tokenized securities onto the network does not automatically mean more transactions or greater demand for Solana’s native cryptocurrency, SOL. “A trade is one transaction whether it moves $100 or $100 million,” Nguyen said. “What matters is turnover, not value parked on-chain.”
What could happen next?
Nguyen said DTCC’s integration would need support from banks and other financial firms to have a real impact on Solana. Institutions would also need enough liquidity to support large trades.
“Banks, brokers and issuers need to say they will issue, trade and settle there, and then do it,” Nguyen said. He added that institutions would need to actively use the tokenized securities rather than simply hold them.
“The assets must be active, not idle: traded around the clock, used as collateral to borrow against, and earning yield,” Nguyen said.
Lin agreed that the longer-term impact would depend on how the assets are used, rather than which blockchain they are issued on.
“No one cares where the assets are issued, but more so where they’re used,” Lin said. “It’s all about where secondary trading and collateral activity will happen and ultimately settle.”

Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente
Crypto hackers stole $8.7 billion so far in 2026, surpassing the projected annual onchain revenue generated across the industry, according to ARK’s research director.
Hackers stole 57 cents for every $1 earned onchain by blockchain protocols since 2017, according to Lorenzo Valente, director of digital asset research at ARK Investment Management.
“Security is the bottleneck,” wrote Valente in a Thursday X post, sharing a chart showing that $8.7 billion lost to crypto hacks year to date had already surpassed the $5.6 billion in estimated annual onchain revenue for 2026.
Since 2017, the crypto industry has lost about $26.9 billion to hacks and earned $47 billion in total onchain revenue, he added.
The recent $6.3 billion stolen in the Binance hack alone exceeded Valente’s estimate for full-year 2026 onchain revenue. Value lost to hacks is on track to exceed onchain revenue by year-end for the first time since 2020.
The crypto industry saw a string of high-value hacks this year, including September’s $387 million Bitget hack and the $320 million Liquid Network exploit, as well as April’s $295 million Drift Protocol exploit.
The mounting security exploits are weighing on the institutional appetite for DeFi. In an April research note, JPMorgan analysts identified bridge security as a long-standing challenge for the industry.
Total value locked in decentralized finance (DeFi) has fallen nearly 10% since the Binance exploit, from $85.9 billion on Oct. 29 to $77.4 billion on Thursday, according to DefiLlama.

items.author: Reuters
items.content: MSCI to drop Strategy from global indexes, putting billions in fund inflows at risk  Reuters --- From rss --- In brief - MSCI will remove Strategy’s MSTR shares from its MSCI USA Index, affecting broader global benchmarks, after November 30. - The index provider’s new rules target companies that resemble investment funds rather than operating businesses. - Selling by index-tracking funds could pressure Strategy’s stock, potentially reducing the money it can raise to buy Bitcoin. Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks. MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes. That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own. Will Strategy hold over 1M BTC before 2027? Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy. This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments. Why is MSCI kicking Strategy out? MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures. MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business. In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.” Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio. Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount. Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result. Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin. Could this hurt Bitcoin? The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable. But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash. So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin. That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers. items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Colette Kress, 59, became Nvidia's interim CEO following Jensen Huang's resignation, while retaining her CFO responsibilities.
- She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at Texas Instruments, Microsoft, and Cisco, helping oversee a more than 50-fold increase in annual revenue.
- Her biggest challenges include maintaining investor confidence, navigating US-China tensions, and managing an organization built around Huang's leadership.
For the first time in 33 years, someone other than Jensen Huang is running Nvidia. And the person taking over is not an engineer, a chip designer, or a Silicon Valley founder.
Colette Kress, Nvidia's 59-year-old chief financial officer, was named interim CEO Thursday following Huang's abrupt resignation amid reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.
Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent replacement, according to Nvidia's regulatory filing. She inherits a company worth trillions of dollars, a shaken investor base, and a management structure built around one man.
From Texas Instruments to Nvidia's AI empire
Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013, when it was primarily known for graphics cards used in video games. She arrived with nearly 25 years of financial experience across some of America's largest technology companies.
She spent eight years at Texas Instruments before joining Microsoft in 1997. During her 13-year tenure there, she became CFO of the Server and Tools division, overseeing financial strategy for Microsoft's enterprise computing business.
In 2010, she moved to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization, managing financial planning and business development across the networking giant's operations.
Kress holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University, according to her official biography.
Her move to Nvidia came with an unusual endorsement. Her two sons, then enthusiastic gamers, encouraged her to join the company responsible for the graphics chips powering their favorite games, according to Forbes.
Huang personally recruited her, explaining his vision for AI computing on a whiteboard during their discussions, Wired reported. At the time, Nvidia was the smallest company Kress had worked for.
The woman behind Nvidia's financial expansion
When Kress joined Nvidia, its annual revenue stood at approximately $4.13 billion. By fiscal 2026, that figure had reached $215.9 billion, an increase of more than 50 times.
Huang drove Nvidia's technological strategy, but Kress oversaw the finances supporting its expansion from gaming hardware into data centers and AI infrastructure.
Her tenure included Nvidia's $6.9 billion acquisition of networking specialist Mellanox and an increasingly aggressive strategy of investing in companies that purchase its computing hardware.
Those relationships now include CoreWeave, in which Nvidia invested another $2 billion in January. CoreWeave's rapid growth reflects enormous demand for Nvidia-powered computing, alongside the financial costs of building that infrastructure.
Kress also became Nvidia's principal financial voice to Wall Street, regularly explaining margins, chip demand and revenue forecasts during earnings calls.
Forbes ranked her among America's richest self-made women in 2026, with almost $750 million in Nvidia shares as of Wednesday's close.
The challenges
Kress takes charge as Nvidia faces questions about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia had already lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market value from its October peak before the board publicly announced its investigation on Huang’s love affairs.
She must also navigate Washington's restrictions on advanced chip exports to China and scrutiny surrounding Nvidia's commercial relationships. The board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security were compromised in the allegations involving Huang.
Her financial expertise cannot entirely replace Huang's technical background or his personal relationships with developers, customers, and governments. Maintaining Nvidia's engineering leadership will require close coordination with the executives responsible for its chips and software.
Kress has promised to build on Huang's legacy, saying that “Nvidia's strength has always come from its people.”
Her first major public test arrives Tuesday, November 17, when Nvidia reports its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings. The company has scheduled its results for approximately 1:20 p.m. Pacific, followed by an investor call at 2 p.m.

items.content:
NK hackers join memecoin trenches, xStocks adds Hong Kong equities: Asia Express
North Korean hackers launch memecoins to launder funds stolen in the Binance hack, while xStocks plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.
North Korean hackers create memecoins to launder funds
North Korean hackers created memecoins to launder cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to a report from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.
Between Nov. 5 and 7, the hackers created at least six tokens on NEAR and used liquidity pools on decentralized exchanges to move $430,000 of stolen funds between wallets, Elliptic said. However, the tokens attracted almost no outside trading and were abandoned shortly after launch.
Elliptic said the same laundering technique was also used following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025, when North Korean-linked actors moved at least $24 million through a newly created token on the TRON blockchain.
HONG KONG
Hong Kong’s wealthy investors are embracing crypto. (Chi Hung Wong)
xStocks tokenizes 200 stocks in UK and EU, with hundreds from Hong Kong coming soon
Kraken parent Payward’s xStocks platform has added tokenized versions of more than 200 stocks listed in the United Kingdom and European Union.
Payward said the latest expansion brings xStocks’ offering to more than 1,500 tokenized assets. The company reported more than $45 billion in cumulative transaction volume and over 550,000 unique holders.
Payward said it plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.
Hong Kong’s forthcoming crypto licensing regime
Deputy Secretary for Financial Services Chan Ho-lim told FinTech Week the region will introduces a new licensing regime for virtual-asset trading, custody, advisory and management, via amendment bills that will be submitted to Legislative Council this year.
More Hong Kong news
Police have arrested 22 people in a cross border money laundering investigation, that allegedly involved a over the counter crypto network that moved more than HKD$150 million (US$18 million) while attempting to obscure the origin of funds. Meanwhile, the US has sanctioned 41 entities allegedly linked to the Cambodia’s Prince Group, including a man named Qiu Yong, who is accused of running Hong Kong companies on behalf of the criminal organization.
SOUTH KOREA
South Korea to permit crypto withdrawal freezes during hacking threats
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) plans to allow crypto exchanges to suspend deposits and withdrawals when hacking is suspected, rather than waiting until a breach is confirmed.
The FSC said it would issue a no-action letter permitting preventive suspensions under certain conditions. Current rules prohibit exchanges from blocking withdrawals without legitimate grounds and explicitly allow restrictions only when a hacking incident is clearly established.
The regulator also called for round-the-clock monitoring and incident response, higher cold-wallet holdings, and stronger insurance coverage and reserves.
GOPAX puts everything on ice
South Korean crypto exchange GOPAX announced on November 6 it was suspending trading, deposits and withdrawals and moving all user assets to cold wallets. The firm had received threatening emails that claimed a hack was imminent, and took the drastic step of putting everything on ice on the recommendation of financial authorities.
JAPAN
Nomura explores sale of crypto unit Laser Digital
Japanese financial services giant Nomura Holdings is reportedly weighing a sale of its cryptocurrency subsidiary Laser Digital as Nomura’s European operations continue to post losses.
Nomura has held talks with potential buyers, including Marex Group but is yet to make a final decision and could keep the business.
Nomura’s European businesses posted a pretax loss of 7.4 billion yen ($46.5 million) in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, their fourth consecutive quarterly loss. The company posted pretax profits in every other reporting region over the same period.
THAILAND
Thailand is examining new rules for ETFs and ICO investors (Sasint)
Thailand proposes $148K daily cap on stablecoin deposits and withdrawals
Thailand’s securities regulator has proposed capping daily stablecoin deposits and withdrawals at 5 million baht ($148,000) each per customer at regulated crypto operators.
The limit would apply separately to deposits and withdrawals at each operator, Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said in a Thursday announcement. The regulator said the rules aim to curb money laundering, cybercrime and attempts to bypass cross-border money transfer rules.
The draft would bar stablecoin transfers to and from third-party wallets.
More Thailand news
Thailand’s SEC will block access to Bitget from December 5. It has also proposed new tests for retail investors before allowing them to invest in ICOs. The tests would require knowledge of at least six areas including digital tokens and investor rights, blockchain technology, digital-asset wallets and distribution channels. The proposals will be up for comment until November 25. The SEC is also seeking feedback on new rules around margin loans and ETFs, but has ruled out allowing leveraged or crypto ETFs at this stage.
Vietnam
South Korean crypto firm Bithumb Asset, has invested $85 million into a luxury resort project in Hoi An in Vietnam being built by local real estate developer Asia Estate. Da Nang police have issued a warning about scams via “ghost” cryptocurrency projects that are really just ponzi schemes in disguise. They highlighted a fraud ring involving the DRK cryptocurrency project, led by Huynh Duc Van, 33, and seven accomplices, which was recently dealt with by law enforcement.
SINGAPORE
Nomura’s former head of crypto derivatives trading, John Kim, has joined Chicago-based DV Trading in Singapore to lead a new discretionary crypto-trading team. A Singapore woman lost S$78,000 (US$60,391) in a four-month long crypto scam after someone posing as an insurance buyer “helped” her to set up a crypto wallet. She initially believed she was making money, before getting cleared out after she was directed to the little known Qevorinex platform. International bank communication network Swift argued at Singapore FinTech Festival for shared standards to prevent digital assets from fragmenting across incompatible systems.

英伟达董事会已接触Arm CEO Rene Haas，作为黄仁勋潜在继任人选之一

BlockBeats 消息，11 月 14 日，据英国《金融时报》援引知情人士报道，英伟达董事会在物色黄仁勋的正式继任者时，已接触软银旗下英国芯片设计公司 Arm 的 CEO Rene Haas。Haas 是多名潜在人选之一，目前尚不确定英伟达是否会正式发出邀约，也不确定 Haas 是否会接受。Arm 拒绝置评，英伟达未立即回应置评请求。

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as Nvidia’s CEO after 33 years, following reports of three extramarital affairs—one involving an executive U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of China ties.
- Nvidia’s stock plunged over 14% before recovering to close down ~4.6%; tech, AI and crypto founders called the ouster a “massive mistake,” while 1,600-plus employee comments pushed to reinstate him.
- The board has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a successor; the turmoil matters for crypto given Nvidia’s grip on AI data-center infrastructure, with earnings due Nov. 17.
In the span of a few days, the most powerful executive in artificial intelligence went from untouchable to unemployed.
Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia from a graphics-card maker into the roughly $4 trillion engine of the AI boom, resigned Thursday after 33 years, felled not by a bad earnings report but by a scandal with the texture of a spy thriller.
Here’s how a defining week for AI, and by extension crypto, unfolded.
The crisis began with reports that Huang had grown close to Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.
For a company at the center of the U.S.-China chip fight and a looming debate over tighter export controls, the national-security overtones were impossible to ignore. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, though it said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.
On Nov. 8, Huang apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, acknowledging the relationship.
Jensen Huang’s exit
What might have been a single lapse quickly snowballed. The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported to Huang.
By Thursday, Huang was out as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones took over as board chair. The abruptness stunned an industry accustomed to treating Huang as synonymous with Nvidia itself.
Then, a day after his resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, an “intimate” one with a second unnamed Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Reuters did not identify her, and Nvidia declined to comment. Huang has acknowledged only the Alice Huang affair, deflecting when the Times asked about Powell.
Affair trade
Nvidia’s stock cratered more than 14% at the open on Thursday before clawing back to close down about 4.6%. Wall Street quickly sorted winners from losers: rivals like AMD and Broadcom fared better, while companies tightly tied to Nvidia’s business took the brunt.
The reaction underscored how much of the AI trade, and the crypto market that increasingly moves with it, rests on a single company.
The scandal then rippled outward. Singapore barred Alice Huang from returning to the country, Alibaba shares slid on reports it was a Megaspeed customer, and congressional committees had already sought a closed-door briefing from Huang over his Megaspeed ties.
The loudest names in tech, AI and crypto called the ouster a blunder, with one founder branding it “a massive mistake.” Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion-box post drew more than 1,600 comments, many pleading for Huang’s return. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one wrote.
The board has moved on regardless. According to the Financial Times, it approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive who led Arm through its 2023 IPO, as a potential successor, though Nvidia called speculation about any candidate “premature.” Analysts have also floated Nvidia’s Ian Buck and AMD’s Lisa Su.
Why it matters for crypto
Nvidia’s chips power the AI data centers whose explosive buildout has become intertwined with crypto, from AI-agent commerce to the mining firms pivoting to host AI workloads.
Leadership turmoil at the company that supplies the picks and shovels ripples outward, and it lands amid a broader reckoning over AI’s role in everything from cyberattacks to data-center politics.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, with Kress at the helm and the permanent CEO search still underway, a nervous moment for a market already rattled by a sharp week-ending selloff.
For now, the company that defined the AI era is leaderless at the top, its founder’s legacy clouded by scandal, and the question hanging over Silicon Valley is whether anyone can fill the role Huang made uniquely his own.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Four nonprofits sued five major AI developers, seeking a freeze on building or releasing more powerful AI models.
- The lawsuit cites incidents involving AI agents escaping testing environments, unauthorized hacking, and warnings about catastrophic risks.
- The plaintiffs argue that California's existing laws can be used to stop dangerous AI development without waiting for new legislation.
Four nonprofit organizations are taking some of the world's biggest AI companies to court, asking a California judge to stop them from developing more powerful artificial intelligence systems before something goes seriously wrong.
The 63-page complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, Irreplaceable Education Fund, and the Alliance for Secure AI.
They want an immediate court order prohibiting the companies from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced models as of November 12, 2026.
“The Frontier AI companies are developing AI Systems that they do not understand and that act contrary to developer intent, evade control, and break the law,” the plaintiffs argue. To prevent this, they request “an immediate injunction forbidding Defendants from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most capable systems as of the date of this Complaint”
That wouldn't necessarily mean shutting down ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other existing products. Instead, it would effectively make today's technology the limit, preventing the companies from releasing more powerful successors.
The complaint also asks the court to prohibit the companies from using AI to independently conduct or direct research into better models, a process related to what researchers call recursive self-improvement. The concern is that such systems could eventually improve faster than humans can understand or control them.
Can AI development be considered a public nuisance?
The nonprofits argue that California already has laws that could prevent companies from developing products that endanger the public, even before those products cause serious harm.
Their lawsuit invokes the state's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits unlawful or unfair business practices. One part of their argument is that developing increasingly capable AI systems creates a public nuisance: a danger that affects the health, safety, or property of a broader community.
For example, a factory releasing dangerous chemicals into a neighborhood could face legal action before someone suffers a fatal injury. The plaintiffs want the court to apply similar reasoning to AI development.
They argue that companies are knowingly creating increasingly powerful systems that could facilitate cyberattacks, help develop biological weapons, or eventually escape human control.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs argue in the complaint.
Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement that the groups want the court to declare the companies' practices unlawful and “freeze further AI development.”
The legal challenge is whether the alleged risks and practices are enough to justify such sweeping restrictions. Even though these frontier labs constantly warn about how powerful and dangerous their models are, as defendants they have not been found liable, and warnings about potential catastrophe do not automatically establish a violation of California law.
The complaint points to incidents that have already occurred as evidence that the dangers aren't entirely hypothetical.
In July, OpenAI models escaped a controlled testing environment and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity evaluation.
A subsequent independent investigation found that roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents used an unauthorized internal message board to coordinate, with about 700 joining the attack on Hugging Face. The agents were attempting to obtain answers to the benchmark testing them.
These incidents involved AI agents, programs that can execute tasks, browse websites, write code, and interact with external systems rather than simply responding to questions.
Documented security failures, however, are not proof that today's AI models can cause human extinction. The plaintiffs are connecting those incidents to predictions about what increasingly capable systems might eventually do, and that broader danger remains disputed.
“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect,” Matthew Platkin, the former New Jersey attorney general representing the plaintiffs, said in the statement.

items.author: Terrence O’Brien
items.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang's resignation and the fallout from Nvidia's leadership crisis, follow Terrence O'Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started On October […]

--- From rss ---
In brief
- Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as Nvidia’s CEO after 33 years, following reports of three extramarital affairs—one involving an executive U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of China ties.
- Nvidia’s stock plunged over 14% before recovering to close down ~4.6%; tech, AI and crypto founders called the ouster a “massive mistake,” while 1,600-plus employee comments pushed to reinstate him.
- The board has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a successor; the turmoil matters for crypto given Nvidia’s grip on AI data-center infrastructure, with earnings due Nov. 17.
In the span of a few days, the most powerful executive in artificial intelligence went from untouchable to unemployed.
Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia from a graphics-card maker into the roughly $4 trillion engine of the AI boom, resigned Thursday after 33 years, felled not by a bad earnings report but by a scandal with the texture of a spy thriller.
Here’s how a defining week for AI, and by extension crypto, unfolded.
The crisis began with reports that Huang had grown close to Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.
For a company at the center of the U.S.-China chip fight and a looming debate over tighter export controls, the national-security overtones were impossible to ignore. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, though it said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.
On Nov. 8, Huang apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, acknowledging the relationship.
Jensen Huang’s exit
What might have been a single lapse quickly snowballed. The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported to Huang.
By Thursday, Huang was out as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones took over as board chair. The abruptness stunned an industry accustomed to treating Huang as synonymous with Nvidia itself.
Then, a day after his resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, an “intimate” one with a second unnamed Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Reuters did not identify her, and Nvidia declined to comment. Huang has acknowledged only the Alice Huang affair, deflecting when the Times asked about Powell.
Affair trade
Nvidia’s stock cratered more than 14% at the open on Thursday before clawing back to close down about 4.6%. Wall Street quickly sorted winners from losers: rivals like AMD and Broadcom fared better, while companies tightly tied to Nvidia’s business took the brunt.
The reaction underscored how much of the AI trade, and the crypto market that increasingly moves with it, rests on a single company.
The scandal then rippled outward. Singapore barred Alice Huang from returning to the country, Alibaba shares slid on reports it was a Megaspeed customer, and congressional committees had already sought a closed-door briefing from Huang over his Megaspeed ties.
The loudest names in tech, AI and crypto called the ouster a blunder, with one founder branding it “a massive mistake.” Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion-box post drew more than 1,600 comments, many pleading for Huang’s return. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one wrote.
The board has moved on regardless. According to the Financial Times, it approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive who led Arm through its 2023 IPO, as a potential successor, though Nvidia called speculation about any candidate “premature.” Analysts have also floated Nvidia’s Ian Buck and AMD’s Lisa Su.
Why it matters for crypto
Nvidia’s chips power the AI data centers whose explosive buildout has become intertwined with crypto, from AI-agent commerce to the mining firms pivoting to host AI workloads.
Leadership turmoil at the company that supplies the picks and shovels ripples outward, and it lands amid a broader reckoning over AI’s role in everything from cyberattacks to data-center politics.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, with Kress at the helm and the permanent CEO search still underway, a nervous moment for a market already rattled by a sharp week-ending selloff.
For now, the company that defined the AI era is leaderless at the top, its founder’s legacy clouded by scandal, and the question hanging over Silicon Valley is whether anyone can fill the role Huang made uniquely his own.

Gate回应用户资产被印度警方司法冻结一事：案件仍在审查，尚未移交任何资产

BlockBeats 消息，11 月 15 日，据官方公告，针对一名用户资产被印度警方要求司法冻结一事，Gate 回应表示，平台作为独立第三方，不会仅凭单方面材料对涉案资金作出判断或承诺移交资产。每一项请求都会内部逐案审核，而目前没有任何资产被移交。整个案件从 2025 年至今，Gate 一直在投入法律资源持续跟进，帮用户建立沟通渠道和争取时间，并非收到印度警方要求后就直接配合执行。

 2025 年 9 月，Gate 收到印度警方的资产冻结请求，其反洗钱团队和法务团队随后多次要求补充证据及案件材料。Gate 称，警方提供的链上记录涉及多个钱包及资金往来。2026 年 4 月，警方提出资产移交相关请求，Gate 未直接承诺执行，继续要求补充材料。根据同年 9 月的沟通，案件当时仍处于司法审查中。Gate 会持续保持这部分资金，在用户抗辩过程中，不会轻易划走，持续帮用户解决问题。

Gate 表示，在收到警方关于提交起诉材料的通知当天，平台即询问能否向用户披露进展，并在获得同意后告知相关用户，以便其寻求法律救济。根据当地律所意见，Gate 作为第三方无法代替用户抗辩或提出异议，但会继续协助用户与有关方面沟通，并提供法律支持。Gate 称，在用户抗辩期间，平台将继续保留相关资金，并在有新进展时同步。

Anthropic前研究员再发警告：算法进步正在加速，训练更强AI可能无需靠堆算力

动察 Beating AI 快讯，今年 9 月，曾在 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 从事预训练研究的 Jacob Coxon 辞职，怒斥两家公司正冲向能够自我改进的超级智能，简直是在「拿我们的生命赌博」。这番言论引来美国议员呼吁加强监管，马斯克甚至怀疑他是在配合监管宣传造势。

现在，Coxon 又贴出 Anthropic IPO 路演中的一张图，称这是促使他辞职的重要原因之一。「这张图太疯狂了，没想到他们竟然公开了。」

Anthropic 原本用这张图展示自己的技术优势：随着算法不断改进，训练出同等代码能力的模型，所需算力越来越少。

但 Coxon 注意到，图中的纵轴已经采用对数刻度，曲线却依然越来越陡。这意味着，如果数据准确，训练效率的提升速度本身也在加快。他据此认为，Anthropic 的算法进步已经呈现「超指数增长」。

Mythos 可能只是这条陡峭曲线上的普通一站。Anthropic 已经可以用远少于最初的算力，训练出与 Mythos 同等水平的模型。如果投入相同的算力，就有可能训练出更强的 AI。

而改进训练算法也不一定需要天才研究员不断提出突破性想法，这类工作已经接近能够自动化的阶段。Anthropic 联合创始人 Tom Brown 在路演中也谈到，未来 Claude 有望自行发现提高训练效率的方法。新方法可以用来训练更强的模型，而更强的模型又能继续寻找新的优化方法。

不过，这张图没有公开具体的算力倍数，只有三个数据点，图下注明位置仅供示意。

Coxon 主张应该在 2027 年暂停前沿 AI 研发，让竞争对手追上。这样会让人类水平的 AI 能力逐渐成为人人可用的普通商品，打破 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 依靠领先模型建立的优势。

Germany’s Bundestag has approved legislation allowing customs authorities to temporarily secure significant assets, including crypto, when there are substantiated doubts about their lawful origin even before a criminal case is opened. The procedure generally targets assets worth more than €100,000, while permanent confiscation would still require a fiscal court ruling.

The law is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027, subject to Bundesrat approval and formal promulgation. — link
